title: What delivery semantics does a streaming pipeline provide (at-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once) and how is exactly-once actually achieved (idempotent producers + transactional writes + checkpointed offsets)?
shortTitle: Delivery semantics and how exactly-once is achieved

s1_definition.profdef: Delivery semantics describe how many times a message may be processed in the presence of failures. At-most-once means each message is processed zero or one time, so it may be lost but never duplicated. At-least-once means each message is processed one or more times, so it is never lost but may be duplicated. Exactly-once means each message affects the result exactly one time despite failures, and it is achieved through a combination of idempotent producers, transactional or idempotent writes, and checkpointed consumer offsets committed atomically with the output.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India posting transfer instructions. At-most-once is like mailing a letter and not keeping a copy: if it gets lost, the transfer never happens, but it is never done twice. At-least-once is like resending the letter until you get a confirmation: the transfer definitely happens, but a slow confirmation might make you send it twice, so Priya could be credited twice. Exactly-once is the bank's gold standard: every transfer happens once and only once, even if systems crash midway, because the bank uses unique instruction numbers and commits the money movement and the "done" mark together in one atomic step so a retry can never double-post.
s1_definition.oneliner: At-most-once may lose, at-least-once may duplicate, and exactly-once applies each message once via idempotent producers, transactional writes, and offsets committed atomically with the output.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Delivery semantics describe how many times a message may be processed in the presence of failures. At-most-once means each message is processed zero or one time, so it may be lost but never duplicated. At-least-once means each message is processed one or more times, so it is never lost but may be duplicated. Exactly-once means each message affects the result exactly one time despite failures, and it is achieved through a combination of idempotent producers, transactional or idempotent writes, and checkpointed consumer offsets committed atomically with the output.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India posting transfer instructions. At-most-once is like mailing a letter and not keeping a copy: if it gets lost, the transfer never happens, but it is never done twice. At-least-once is like resending the letter until you get a confirmation: the transfer definitely happens, but a slow confirmation might make you send it twice, so Priya could be credited twice. Exactly-once is the bank's gold standard: every transfer happens once and only once, even if systems crash midway, because the bank uses unique instruction numbers and commits the money movement and the "done" mark together in one atomic step so a retry can never double-post.

**One line to remember:** At-most-once may lose, at-least-once may duplicate, and exactly-once applies each message once via idempotent producers, transactional writes, and offsets committed atomically with the output.

sections.s2_technical:
The three semantics are really a trade-off between the risk of loss and the risk of duplication, forced by the reality that networks and processes fail at the worst moments. At-most-once is the simplest: the consumer commits its offset before processing, so if it crashes mid-processing, the message is already marked done and is skipped on restart. Nothing is duplicated, but messages can be lost, which is acceptable only for data you can afford to drop, like some metrics, and never for money.

At-least-once commits the offset only after processing succeeds, so if the consumer crashes after processing but before committing, it reprocesses that message on restart. Nothing is lost, but the same message can be applied more than once, which is the default for most systems because losing data is usually worse than duplicating it. The catch is that duplicates are deadly in finance: applying a debit twice is wrong. The usual remedy is to make downstream effects idempotent so a duplicate has no additional effect.

Exactly-once means the observable result reflects each message once, even though internally the engine may retry. It is not magic; it is engineered from three cooperating pieces. First, idempotent producers ensure that a producer retry does not write the same record twice into the log; the broker deduplicates using a producer id and sequence number. Second, transactional or idempotent writes ensure the output side applies each record once; either the sink supports a transaction that commits output and consumer offsets together, or the write is naturally idempotent via an upsert keyed by a stable id. Third, checkpointed offsets tie it together: the consumer's position is committed atomically with the output, so on recovery the engine resumes from a point consistent with what was actually written, never reprocessing already-committed effects nor losing in-flight ones. Flink achieves this with checkpoint barriers and a two-phase commit sink; Kafka achieves read-process-write exactly-once with transactions that commit produced messages and consumed offsets atomically.

A senior nuance is that exactly-once is usually end-to-end only within systems that support the needed transactions, and crossing into an external system that cannot participate often reduces you to at-least-once plus idempotent writes, which is the pragmatic pattern in many banks. The key insight is that even where true transactional exactly-once is unavailable, you can get effectively-once results by combining at-least-once delivery with idempotent, upsert-by-id writes, so a replay or retry overwrites rather than duplicates. The choice is deliberate: for money movement and balances you insist on exactly-once or effectively-once; for low-value telemetry you may accept at-least-once or even at-most-once to save cost and complexity.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A debit must never be lost and never applied twice even if the consumer crashes and retries. This is exactly the exactly-once requirement.

Problem 2 — At-least-once delivery will replay a message after a crash. This is exactly why downstream writes must be idempotent.

Problem 3 — The offset and the output must agree after recovery. This is exactly committing offsets atomically with the write.

The mini-project simulates all three semantics on the same debit. `Processor` applies a debit to an account ledger. `AtMostOnce` commits offset before processing (can lose on crash). `AtLeastOnce` commits after processing (can duplicate on crash). `ExactlyOnce` uses an idempotent apply keyed by message id plus atomic offset-and-output commit, so a simulated crash-and-replay neither loses nor duplicates. The demo injects a crash after processing but before commit and shows each semantic's outcome on Rajesh's balance.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is one debit message M1 for 50000 against Rajesh's account (SAV2001), opening balance 1000000, with a simulated crash at the critical moment for each semantic.

Step 1 — At-most-once. The consumer commits the offset first, then crashes before actually processing. On restart the offset is already past M1, so the debit is skipped entirely. Rajesh's balance stays at 1000000 because the debit was lost. No duplication, but data loss.

Step 2 — At-least-once. The consumer processes the debit first, reducing the balance to 950000, then crashes before committing the offset. On restart M1 is reprocessed because its offset was never committed, applying the 50000 debit a second time and dropping the balance to 900000. No loss, but a wrong double-debit.

Step 3 — Exactly-once setup. The consumer uses an idempotent apply keyed by the message id M1 and will commit the offset atomically with the output. It processes M1, reducing the balance to 950000, and records M1 as applied.

Step 4 — Exactly-once crash and replay. The consumer crashes before the atomic commit, so on restart M1 is retried. But the ledger already recorded M1 as applied, so the idempotent apply detects the duplicate and skips it, leaving the balance at 950000.

Step 5 — Compare outcomes. At-most-once lost the debit (balance 1000000), at-least-once double-applied it (balance 900000), and exactly-once applied it precisely once (balance 950000). Only exactly-once is correct for money, achieved by idempotent writes plus atomic offset-and-output commit.

```
INFO: === AT-MOST-ONCE (crash loses the debit) ===
SEVERE: CRASH after commit, before processing → message LOST
INFO: Rajesh balance = 1000000.00 (debit lost)
INFO: === AT-LEAST-ONCE (crash duplicates the debit) ===
INFO: debit 50000.00 → balance 950000.00
SEVERE: CRASH after processing, before commit → will REPROCESS on restart
INFO: debit 50000.00 → balance 900000.00
INFO: Rajesh balance = 900000.00 (debited TWICE — wrong)
INFO: === EXACTLY-ONCE (crash is safe) ===
INFO: debitOnce 50000.00 → balance 950000.00
SEVERE: CRASH before atomic commit → replay will retry the SAME msgId
WARNING: SKIP duplicate msg M1 (idempotent)
INFO: Rajesh balance = 950000.00 (debited exactly once — correct)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  One debit M1 (SAV2001 -50000), crash at the critical moment
    │
    ├─ AT-MOST-ONCE            ├─ AT-LEAST-ONCE          ├─ EXACTLY-ONCE
    │  commit offset FIRST     │  process FIRST          │  idempotent apply by msgId
    │  crash → skip on restart │  crash before commit    │  + atomic offset+output commit
    │  debit LOST              │  → reprocess → DUPLICATE │  crash → replay deduped

  balance 1,000,000           balance 900,000           balance 950,000
  (lost)                      (double — wrong)          (exactly once — correct)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Delivery semantics describe how many times a message may be processed when failures happen, and they are a trade-off between losing data and duplicating it. At-most-once commits the offset before processing, so a crash in the middle means the message is skipped on restart; nothing is duplicated but messages can be lost, which is only acceptable for data you can afford to drop. At-least-once commits the offset after processing succeeds, so a crash after processing but before committing causes reprocessing on restart; nothing is lost but the message can be applied more than once, which is the common default because losing data is usually worse than duplicating it. Exactly-once means the observable result reflects each message once despite internal retries.

Exactly-once is not magic; it is engineered from three cooperating pieces. Idempotent producers ensure a producer retry does not write the same record twice into the log, because the broker deduplicates using a producer id and sequence number. Transactional or idempotent writes ensure the output side applies each record once, either through a sink transaction that commits output and offsets together or through an upsert keyed by a stable id. And checkpointed offsets tie it together by committing the consumer's position atomically with the output, so on recovery the engine resumes from a point consistent with what was actually written. Flink does this with checkpoint barriers and a two-phase commit sink, and Kafka does read-process-write exactly-once with transactions that commit produced messages and consumed offsets atomically. A senior point I add is that when you cross into an external system that cannot participate in those transactions, you often drop to at-least-once plus idempotent upserts, which gives effectively-once results.

In my project at the National Bank of India this distinction was the difference between correct and catastrophic. For a debit message, at-most-once could lose the debit, and at-least-once could apply it twice and wrongly reduce Rajesh's balance by a hundred thousand instead of fifty. So for money movement we insisted on exactly-once or effectively-once: idempotent writes keyed by a stable message id meant a replay after a crash simply skipped the already-applied debit, and the offset was committed atomically with the output so recovery never reprocessed committed effects. For low-value telemetry we were happy with at-least-once to save complexity, but for balances and transfers nothing less than exactly-once was acceptable.
